narrative.text: The foreword by the WHO Director-General, which places digital technologies in the long history of health advances and gives examples such as rapid diagnostics, 3-D printing, telemedicine and artificial intelligence. It presents the guideline as evidence to help countries invest wisely and stresses that digital tools are means to promote health and serve the vulnerable, not ends in themselves.

The acknowledgements, naming the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research staff who coordinated the guideline, the Norwegian Institute of Public Health team that gave methodological support, and the many WHO staff and regional advisers involved. It also credits the designers and lists the funders, stating that they did not influence the content.
A list of abbreviations used in the guideline, covering terms such as GRADE, PICO, mHealth, SMS and the names of organizations including ITU, UNFPA, UNICEF and USAID.

The executive summary of the guideline, which defines eHealth, mHealth and digital health and recalls the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution asking WHO for normative guidance on evidence-based digital interventions. It warns that enthusiasm has led to many short-lived implementations with little evaluation of benefits and harms. Using an adapted Tanahashi model, it explains how health system shortfalls limit universal health coverage and how digital interventions might address them. It ends with a figure linking ten recommendations, on birth and death notification, stock notification, telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support, digital tracking and training, to the health system challenges they address.

Introduces the background to the guideline, defining eHealth, mHealth and digital health and noting the strong interest in digital health in low- and middle-income countries, with over a thousand implementations recorded since 2008. It cites the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution and the Bellagio eHealth evaluation statement, stressing the need to assess effects and avoid diverting resources from non-digital approaches.

Explains the role of digital health in strengthening health systems and universal health coverage using the Tanahashi framework, which shows how system performance is lost at successive levels such as availability, accessibility, acceptance and effective coverage. It describes how digital interventions aimed at clients, health workers, managers and data services can address these challenges. A figure links health system challenges, digital interventions from the WHO classification and ICT systems, using commodity stock notification as an example.

States that the guideline responds to the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on digital health and aims to give recommendations based on critical appraisal of evidence on benefits, harms, acceptability, feasibility, resource use and equity. It lists the digital interventions covered, including birth and death notification, stock management, telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support, digital tracking and health worker training.

Identifies the main audience as health ministry decision-makers and public health professionals, as well as implementing and development partners, and notes that the recommended interventions, though reviewed for mobile devices, can be used on any digital device.

Explains that WHO had not previously issued normative guidance specifically on digital health interventions, and lists WHO clinical guidelines that already include digital elements, such as those on HIV, TB and community health workers. It also describes related WHO resources, including the classification of digital health interventions, the Digital Health Atlas and the Be He@lthy, Be Mobile initiative with ITU.

Describes how the maturity of the enabling environment and ICT environment, including leadership, governance, policy, financing, workforce, standards and interoperability, affects the impact of digital interventions. It cautions that adopting the recommendations must not undermine quality care where digital tools are unavailable or unaccepted, and that weak ecosystems should first be strengthened.

Stresses that digital interventions should fit into a coherent digital health architecture rather than operate as isolated duplicates. It points to complementary resources such as the WHO/ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit and the ITU Digital Health Platform Handbook, and lists communities of practice including the African Alliance, AeHIN and OpenHIE.

Describes the living guideline approach, under which this first version covers a priority list of mobile-accessible digital interventions and later versions will add further interventions and health areas as evidence emerges. It gives the example of extending targeted client communication to noncommunicable diseases.

Summarizes the methods used, following the WHO handbook for guideline development, with two online surveys and three meetings held in February 2016, September 2016 and June 2018 to set the scope, prioritize questions and formulate recommendations.

Describes how priority questions were identified, starting from the WHO classification of digital health interventions and its list of health system challenges, and drafted in PICO format. It explains that questions were refined at a virtual consultation and scoping meeting and ranked through two surveys of more than 300 respondents from all WHO regions.

Lists the nine digital health interventions prioritized for evidence review, from birth and death notification to telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support, digital tracking and health worker training. Table 2.1 defines each intervention with synonyms, and the text describes the outcomes considered. It notes that the reviews focused on mobile access for low-resource settings without excluding other devices. No restrictions were placed on delivery channels such as voice, text messages or interactive voice response.

Explains the two types of evidence considered: effectiveness evidence from randomized trials and other controlled studies, and qualitative evidence on acceptability, feasibility and implementation. It notes that cost evidence came only from included studies and programme documents, and describes an overarching analysis of cross-cutting factors from qualitative reviews and other syntheses.

Describes how risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane and EPOC criteria for effectiveness studies and a critical appraisal tool for qualitative studies. It explains how certainty of effectiveness evidence was graded and how confidence in qualitative findings was rated with the CERQual approach as high, moderate, low or very low.

Sets out the roles of the groups that developed the guideline, including the WHO steering group drawn from many departments, the technical team, the Guideline Development Group, the external review group and observers. It also explains how declarations of interest were collected and managed, with a summary given in Annex 4 and member biographies published online.

Explains, in the Spanish edition of WHO's guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening, how evidence profiles were consolidated into evidence-to-decision frameworks. Each question was judged on effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, resource use, and gender, equity and rights to guide the guideline group's decisions.

Describes how the guideline development group received evidence-to-decision frameworks and GRADE profiles before its final in-person meeting and aimed for majority decisions on each recommendation. It outlines the steps of presentation, discussion and voting on each criterion and on the recommendation category. It also defines the recommendation categories and explains how members with conflicts of interest were handled.

Explains how the draft guideline was written after the final meeting, reviewed by the guideline group and external peer reviewers, limited to factual and language corrections afterwards, and sent back to members for approval.
Explains that the recommendations appear in the executive summary, with evidence summaries in Chapter 3, and that relevant existing WHO recommendations are quoted exactly with contextual remarks.

Introduces the chapter of evidence-based recommendations, which this Spanish text numbers as nine, on prioritised digital health interventions. It lists what is given for each intervention and points to annexes and web supplements for evidence gaps and evidence-to-decision frameworks.

Summarises cross-cutting qualitative findings on the acceptability and feasibility of digital interventions used by health workers, based on evidence syntheses. It covers factors that may raise or lower acceptability for health workers and practical feasibility issues. Findings on clients and their concerns are also included. The end of the block begins the section on birth and death notification and its links to civil registration.

Covers digital birth and death notification, listing health system challenges such as missing population denominators and delays in reporting events. It notes that wider access to mobile devices among community actors can extend civil registration coverage and summarises the evidence. WHO recommends digital birth notification where it gives individual-level data to a system able to respond, and digital death notification only in the context of rigorous research under similar conditions. Implementation considerations include linking birth notification to high-coverage services such as immunisation while checking that registration systems can absorb more notifications.

Covers digital stock notification and commodity management, explaining the importance of commodity availability for quality care and universal health coverage and the problem of stock-outs. It summarises the evidence and implementation issues. WHO recommends the intervention where supply chain systems can respond promptly and appropriately to notifications, despite limited evidence of effectiveness. The block ends by introducing telemedicine as a way to improve access to health facilities and staff.

Covers client-to-provider telemedicine as a response to geographic barriers, shortages of qualified staff and care delays, describing forms such as remote monitoring and store-and-forward exchange. It mentions WHO's 2010 global report on telemedicine and summarises the evidence. WHO recommends it only as a complement to face-to-face care and where patient safety, privacy, traceability and accountability can be monitored. The block ends by introducing provider-to-provider telemedicine.

Covers provider-to-provider telemedicine as a response to geographic barriers and shortages or limited skills of health workers, with a summary of the evidence. WHO recommends it where patient safety, privacy, traceability and accountability can be monitored, including procedures for consent and data protection. Implementation considerations follow.

Covers targeted client communication through mobile devices for behaviour change on sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health, addressing challenges such as low demand and loss to follow-up. It summarises the evidence on effects and acceptability across population groups. WHO recommends this intervention provided that confidentiality and data privacy concerns are properly addressed. The block ends by introducing health worker decision support.

Covers digital decision support for health workers, addressing poor guideline adherence, inadequate referrals and limited competence. It notes that decision support tools are well established and increasingly delivered on mobile devices, and summarises the evidence. WHO recommends decision support for tasks already within health workers' defined scope of practice. The block ends by introducing digital tracking of clients' health status and services.

Covers digital tracking of clients' health status and services, alone and combined with decision support and targeted client communication, addressing gaps in continuity of care and coverage. It summarises the evidence for each combination. WHO recommends digital tracking with decision support, and with decision support plus targeted communication, where the health system can support integrated implementation and for tasks within health workers' scope of practice. The block ends by introducing mobile learning for health workers.

Covers digital delivery of training and educational content to health workers through mobile learning, with a summary of the evidence. WHO recommends it provided it complements, rather than replaces, traditional continuing education and in-service training. Implementation considerations are set out.

Notes that digital health shares underlying problems of other health system interventions, such as weak management, poor training and infrastructure limits, so context and the enabling environment are crucial.

Explains how the different digital health recommendations meet health system needs in connected ways, from commodity availability for managers to access to information and services for clients. A figure shows how notification, telemedicine, targeted communication, decision support and mobile learning together support accountable, high-quality care.

Describes the four core components of digital health implementations in the Spanish edition of WHO's guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening: accurate health content aligned with recommended practice, the digital health intervention itself, the digital applications that deliver it, and the ICT and enabling environment. A figure shows how these components fit together with governance, legislation, workforce, standards and infrastructure.

Stresses that digital health implementations must be adapted to local needs, users and the wider ecosystem, pointing to the WHO/ITU National eHealth strategy toolkit for assessing readiness and tabulating its enabling-environment components. It sets out practical considerations under headings such as leadership and governance, strategy and investment, legislation and compliance (privacy, consent, data security), standards and interoperability, infrastructure, workforce and health content. It closes with human rights, equity and gender considerations, including keeping non-digital services for those excluded, and the Principles for Digital Development.

Introduces the chapter on future research, which covers cross-cutting evidence gaps on effectiveness, resource use and human rights, equity and gender, as well as research questions specific to each intervention.

Sets out general research gaps in digital health where evidence was of low or very low certainty, often due to poor reporting, small studies and limited settings. It calls for studies measuring both health system process improvements and distal health outcomes while tracking technical performance and user engagement, along with longer-term costing and cost-effectiveness research. It also highlights the need to study effects on equity and inequalities and implementation research on combinations of interventions, fidelity at scale and frameworks such as RE-AIM.

Lists issues for designing future evaluations of digital health interventions, such as using alternative designs like stepped-wedge or interrupted time-series studies for complex system-level interventions and measuring intermediate outcomes. It also notes that software changes during evaluation call for parallel process evaluations and shared tools and metrics for effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.
A heading fragment reading 'of the guideline', with no further content.

Describes how WHO will disseminate the digital health guideline in full and condensed forms through regional offices and networks such as AeHIN, the Global Digital Health Network and the Health Data Collaborative, as well as consultations and webinars. It also mentions a forthcoming WHO and PATH planning and costing guide to help ministries implement the recommended interventions.

Explains that the guideline will follow a living-guideline approach, with new evidence reviewed by the guideline development group and a first update adding targeted client communication for noncommunicable diseases in version 1.1. It anticipates a major update within 18–24 months and continued work with WHO's Guidelines Review Committee.
A glossary of digital health terms used in the guideline, including digital health application, digital health architecture, eHealth, client, mHealth and digital health.
The reference list for the digital health guideline, citing mainly WHO reports and resolutions on eHealth and mHealth, GSMA resources, systematic reviews and digital health network websites.

Annex 1, reproducing WHO's Classification of digital health interventions v1.0, which groups interventions for clients, health workers, health system managers and data services and maps them to health system challenges such as insufficient supply, low demand and loss to follow-up.

Annex 2, a table of the priority questions in PICO format addressed by the guideline, covering interventions such as birth and death notification via mobile devices, stock management, telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support and mobile learning. For each it lists populations, comparators and outcomes such as data use, efficiency, service use, unintended consequences, satisfaction and cost-effectiveness.

Annex 3, listing contributors to the guideline, including the guideline development group co-chaired by Pascale Allotey and Alain Labrique with members from many countries and organizations. It also names members of the WHO steering group from headquarters departments and regional offices.

Annex 4, summarizing declarations of interest by guideline development group members and how each was handled. Most members declared no interests, while those who led systematic reviews or had related funding were excluded from final votes on the relevant recommendations.

Annex 5, presenting evidence maps that show mostly low or very low quality evidence for the effectiveness of the digital interventions reviewed, with tables by intervention and outcome type for clients, health workers and health systems. It also tabulates specific research gaps and illustrative research questions, such as the costs and cost-effectiveness of mobile learning. It notes that resource use and cost-effectiveness are cross-cutting gaps for all interventions, and ends with WHO's Geneva address.

Front matter of the Spanish edition of the WHO guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening, beginning with the title page. It includes the 2022 copyright and cataloguing page with ISBNs, Creative Commons licence terms and standard disclaimers. A table of contents follows, listing the chapters, annexes on contributors, declarations of interest and evidence maps, and English-only web supplements with GRADE tables and evidence-to-decision frameworks.
